## Can AI Agents Answer Your Data Questions? A Benchmark for Data Agents

Ruiying Ma 1 * , Shreya Shankar 1 * , Ruiqi Chen 2 , Adit Chintamaneni 1 , Yiming Lin 1 , Sepanta Zeighami 1 , Rajoshi Ghosh 3 , Abhinav Gupta 3 , Anushrut Gupta 3 , Tanmai Gopal 3 , Aditya G. Parameswaran 1

1 UC Berkeley, 2 University of Washington, 3 Hasura PromptQL

{ruiyingm, shreyashankar, adityagp}@berkeley.edu

## Abstract

Users across enterprises increasingly rely on LLM agents to query their data through natural language. However, building reliable data agents remains difficult because real enterprise data is fragmented across many heterogeneous database systems, with duplicated and inconsistent data, and key information often buried in unstructured text-requiring agents to go beyond just writing SQL or data science scripts to answer questions. Existing benchmarks tackle only individual pieces of this end-toend workflow-e.g., text-to-SQL over a single database-and are increasingly saturated and contaminated. We present a new benchmark for LLM agents, the Data Agent Benchmark (DAB), grounded in a study of enterprises building production data agents across six industries. DAB comprises 104 queries across 17 datasets and 4 database management systems. On DAB, the best state-of-the-art agent achieves only 57% pass@1. We analyze agent failure modes and distill takeaways for future data-agent development. Our benchmark and experiment code are published at github.com/ucbepic/DataAgentBench .

## 1 Introduction

Users across enterprises increasingly want data agents , or AI agents that answer natural-language questions over their data. Data agents are a major application of LLMs and a new workload pattern for data systems [31]: major database vendors have added agent capabilities to their platforms [12, 40], and organizations have invested heavily in building their own-for example, Uber's QueryGPT handles over 1.2 million interactive queries per month [43], and OpenAI built an internal data agent used by thousands of employees to query 70,000 datasets totaling 600 petabytes [44].

* Co-first authors.

Yet building reliable data agents is hard. Consider an example query for a data agent: a sales analyst asks, 'Which leads from last quarter should we follow up on?' Answering this requires finding lead records in a customer relationship management (CRM) tool, matching them against call transcripts stored in a separate document database, classifying each lead's intent from unstructured text, and applying domain knowledge about what makes a lead good to pursue. In fact, enterprise data is well-known to be fragmented and messy: surveys find that 72% of organizations store data in disparate silos [41] and 82% report that these silos disrupt critical workflows [19].

Unfortunately, no benchmark measures end-toend data agent capabilities. For example, text-toSQLbenchmarks [8, 26, 28, 47] test whether LLMs can translate a natural-language question into a single correct query over a single relational database, but do not require multi-step reasoning or integration across different databases. Table questionanswering (Table-QA) benchmarks [9, 10] provide tiny tables entirely in the prompt-unlike enterprise workloads, where tables live in databases and rarely fit in context. Moreover, the public benchmarks in this space are increasingly saturated by frontier models, and reported scores are further confounded by two issues: data contamination of public test sets in pretraining [38], and pervasive annotation errors that inflate accuracy-error rates reach 52.8% in BIRD Mini-Dev and 62.8% in Spider-Snow [21].

The Data Agent Benchmark (DAB). We present DAB, a new benchmark for evaluating AI agents on realistic, complex data-oriented tasks. DAB comprises 104 natural-language queries across 17 datasets and 4 database management systems (DBMSes). The size of DAB is comparable to other carefully-curated agent benchmarks (e.g., FrontierMath [13], TerminalBench [32]). Each DAB query requires an agent to interact with a

full environment using database and Python tools, potentially involving hundreds of reasoning and action steps. This differs substantially from largescale benchmarks such as Text-to-SQL, where each item typically requires a single LLM call (e.g., to generate one SQL query). DAB has been publicly available 1 for five months and has already attracted 29 submissions.

Building DAB took us over a year and involved three core challenges. The first challenge was to solicit aspects of production workloads that make data-agent queries difficult. Through a formative study with six enterprises building production data agents (Section 3.1), we identified four properties that are unaddressed by existing benchmarks: (i) the data needed to answer a query is distributed across multiple heterogeneous database systems, (ii) identifiers for the same entity are formatted differently across databases, (iii) answers are buried in unstructured text fields and cannot be retrieved via SQL, and (iv) the query requires domain knowledge not inferable from the data alone (e.g., finance jargon).

The second challenge was to translate these properties into a reproducible benchmark. Since enterprise data is proprietary, we had to build DAB from open-source data-which is typically cleanto mirror the dirty, duplicated, and inconsistently formatted data we observed in production. We also had to ensure there is a deterministic, unambiguous ground-truth answer for each query.

The third challenge was calibrating difficulty: DABshould be hard enough to discriminate among agents, but not so hard that no agent succeeds.

[1 https://ucbepic.github.io/ DataAgentBench/](https://ucbepic.github.io/DataAgentBench/)

We spent $4,346 to evaluate three state-of-the-art frontier agents and harnesses-Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (Claude Code), GPT-5.5 (Codex), and Gemini-3.1Pro (ReAct)-each under three experimental variants: no assistance, with database and schema descriptions added, and with both descriptions and hints describing how the data was corrupted. The best agent reaches only 57% pass@1 (5 trials per query), and most datasets show partial accuracy across agents, leaving headroom for improvement. We further analyze trajectories and provide a taxonomy of failure modes. 90% of wrong answers stem from incorrect planning or faulty implementation rather than wrong data selection; and agents rely almost exclusively on regular expressions for free-text extraction, with only one agent attempting alternatives like using NLP parsing libraries or spawning subagents to extract values in context.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

1. We characterize real-world data-agent workloads via a study with six enterprises building data agents, and identify four properties that distinguish them from the queries existing benchmarks cover.
2. We construct and release DAB, a new benchmark of 104 queries across 17 datasets and 4 database systems.
3. We evaluate state-of-the-art agents on DAB and find that even the best agent achieves only 57% pass@1; our error analysis surfaces failure modes that point to concrete directions for improving data agents.

## 2 Related Work

Despite databases being among the most ubiquitous professional tools, no frontier-model evaluation in- cludes a database-use benchmark. We position DAB against a few categories of benchmarks, summarized in Table 1.

Tool-use benchmarks. Tool-use benchmarks evaluate LLM agents on external tools such as function calling [37], code editing [20], browser interaction [51], command-line tasks [32], and multi-step web reasoning [33], but none involves querying a database. Closer to our setting, benchmarks for data-adjacent workflows such as retail customer service [46] and CRM operations [17] expose each data operation through a hand-crafted API endpoint-the agent never queries the underlying database directly.

Data-related benchmarks. Other benchmarks target data tasks directly, yet each captures only part of the data-agent workflow.

Table question-answering. Table QA benchmarks supply data in the prompt and ask the model to reason over in-context tables [9, 10, 35, 42, 52]; some add unstructured text, as in HybridQA [9], or domain knowledge, as in FinQA [10]. Because tables are given in context, the agent never queries a database, and real-world tables routinely exceed context-window limits.

Text-to-SQL. Text-to-SQL benchmarks instead have the model generate a query for a naturallanguage question over a single databaseSpider [47], WikiSQL [50], and BIRD [28], with extensions to multi-turn dialogue [48] and cloud SQL dialects [26]. This setup is limited: it tests only SQL generation over a single clean database, whereas enterprise questions typically span multiple systems and require transformations that SQL cannot express. Even within this narrow setting, text-to-SQL performance on data-warehouse tasks over private data is abysmal [8]. These text-to-SQL benchmarks are also saturated and corrupted: top systems reach 91.2% execution accuracy on Spider [47], and the reported scores are confounded by data contamination-the public test sets appear in pretraining corpora [38]-and by annotation errors, with error rates of 52.8% in BIRD Mini-Dev and 62.8% in Spider 2.0-Snow [21].

Data science and engineering. Beyond SQL, other benchmarks task the agent with analyzing data, but over flat files (e.g., CSVs) rather than databases. DS-1000 [24], DA-Code [18], and KramaBench [23] require multi-step code over such files, while Spider 2-V [5] requires operating data-engineering tools through GUI actions

| Benchmark                   | (i)   | (ii)   | (iii)   | (iv)   |
|-----------------------------|-------|--------|---------|--------|
| General tool-use [20, 37]   | ✗     | ✗      | ✗       | ◦      |
| Table QA [9, 10]            | ✗     | ✗      | ✔       | ◦      |
| Text-to-SQL [26, 28]        | ✗     | ✗      | ✗       | ◦      |
| Data science &eng. [18, 23] | ✗     | ✗      | ✗       | ✗      |
| Semantic query processing   | ✗     | ✗      | ✔       | ✗      |

(e.g., configuring an Airbyte sync). Neither setting requires querying a database directly.

Semantic query processing. Semantic query processing extends relational operators with naturallanguage variants powered by LLMs [22, 29, 30, 36, 39]. Benchmarks such as SemBench [25] and TAG-Bench [4] execute a pre-constructed pipeline of these operators over flat files to obtain a single answer, but do not capture multi-system integration. The semantic operations in DAB are a subset of those these benchmarks evaluate, embedded within an end-to-end querying workflow over real database systems.

Overall, each of these benchmarks covers only a slice of data work, and many prescribe the exact tools or operations the agent must use. DAB takes a different view: it specifies a realistic data setup-multiple databases with messiness seen in production workloads-and places no restrictions on how the agent solves the task.

## 3 Benchmark Construction

## 3.1 Formative Study

We conducted a study (approximately two months of interviews and analysis) with six enterprises building production data agents across six industries (technology, finance, food services, ecommerce, SaaS, and healthcare). The interview protocol and an anonymized summary of one enterprise's response are in Section A.1. We performed a thematic analysis [11] of the responses to find recurring patterns of challenges, and came up with the following four properties of the workloads that should be in DAB:

- (i) multi-database integration : a single question may require querying across several databases with different query language dialects (e.g., SQL dialects and MongoDB's query language).

(ii) ill-formatted join keys : identifiers for the same entity may be formatted differently across databases-e.g., a book ID appearing as bid\_123

in one table and bref\_123 in another-requiring the agent to detect and reconcile the mismatch before joining.

- (iii) unstructured text transformation : answers may be embedded in text fields that the agent must parse into structured values before they can be filtered, grouped, or joined.
- (iv) domain knowledge : answering the query correctly requires expertise not inferable from the data alone, such as knowing that stock volatility must be computed from adjusted closing prices to account for splits and dividends.

We exclude two common types of queries: those that depend on live external APIs, and open-ended queries (e.g., 'why are my sales going down?'), since neither admits a single stable ground-truth answer.

## 3.2 Construction

Table 2 details the 17 datasets in DAB with a representative query each. Because the enterprises' data is proprietary, we build DAB from open-source datasets whose queries instantiate the four properties identified above. Every query in DAB involves (i) and at least one of (ii) or (iii); (iv) appears in proportion to its prevalence in the study. Constructing DAB took approximately eight months of author time, averaging roughly 50 hours per dataset to collect the source data, design and corrupt it, write the queries, and validate the ground-truth answers.

Datasets. Figure 2 illustrates the four-step dataset

- creation procedure; we walk through them, using the bookreview dataset as a running example.
- (1) Collect open-source datasets. We collect open-source datasets that have multiple tables (so we can later distribute them across databases) and at least one unstructured text column (so we can later embed answer-revealing values into it). Four of the 17 datasetsagnews [49], crmarenapro [17], imdb [27], and krama [23]-come from existing benchmarks; we sample their queries (rewriting some to remove ambiguity). The remaining 14 are sourced from open data repositories. For example, bookreview consists of a books\_info table (with an unstructured description fi eld) and a separate reviews table.
- (2) Induce ill-formatted join keys (property ii) and unstructured-text transformation (property iii). We remove columns that would trivially answer a query and re-embed their values elsewhere, so the agent must work to recover them. Four example strategies include:
- Renaming a shared identifier across tables. The same identifier appears under different column names in the two tables it joins. For example, in bookreview , the book identifier is book\_id in the books\_info table (PostgreSQL) but purchase\_id in the review table (SQLite); to join the two, the agent must recognize that these columns refer to the same entity.
- Applying many row-specific corruptions to a column. For some datasets we apply one of several corruption methods row-by-row to the same col-

Figure 2: Dataset creation methodology, illustrated on the bookreview dataset. Step 1: collect an open-source dataset with two tables, books\_info and reviews . Step 2: transform the data by removing publishedDate and publisher and re-embedding their values into a new details column via LLM-generated sentences, and by prefixing the join keys ( id → bid , book\_id → bref ). Step 3: distribute the tables across PostgreSQL and SQLite. Step 4: create a dataset description ( descriptions.txt ) and a hints file ( hints.txt ).

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

umn, with so many variants per row that no small regex can clean the column: the agent has to inspect every row to figure out the cleaning logic. The methods include:

- (a) prepending a different domain-relevant word to each value, generated by a coding agent (Claude Code) that produces thousands of plausible words per dataset. For usaspending , these words resemble agency codes, fiscal-year tags, or program identifiers (e.g., FY2023\_ , DOD-, PROG/ ).

(b) applying per-character OCR-like substitutions ( 0 ↔ O , 1 ↔ I , 5 ↔ S , etc.) with some probability ( ∼ 0 . 1 per character).

We apply these methods independently in each table where the column appears. For example, in usaspending , the award\_id column is corrupted with OCR substitutions, applied independently in the contracts and recipients tables; to join the two, the agent must essentially perform entity resolution on the award\_id column.

- Hiding answer-revealing values in a text column. We prompt GPT-4o to rewrite a free-text column so it mentions the value in prose ('transform {free\_text} to naturally include a reference to {value}; change as little as possible'), then
- drop the original column. For example, in bookreview , publishedDate , publisher , and language are embedded into details and removed from books\_info .
- Encoding a numeric column as varied free text. We convert a numeric column into a free-text column where each row's value is written differently, requiring the agent to do data cleaning to recover the underlying number. For example, in usaspending , the contract award amount is stored as text where one row might read 1500000 , another $1,500,000 , another 1.5M , another one million five hundred thousand dollars , and another a sum-of-parts expression like $1,050,000 + $450,000 .
- (3) Distribute tables across DBMSes (property i: multi-database integration). We split each dataset's tables across at least two DBMSes, deciding placement manually to mirror how enterprises typically organize data: transaction-oriented tables (records, profiles, reviews) go in row-oriented or document stores (PostgreSQL, MongoDB, SQLite), analytics-oriented tables (large fact tables, time series) go in the columnar store DuckDB, and large free-text or document corpora (e.g., article bodies, review collections) go in MongoDB. The agent must therefore handle MongoDB's query language alongside SQL dialects. For example, bookreview 's book metadata table books\_info goes in PostgreSQL and its reviews table in SQLite.
- (4) Provide a natural-language description and hints file (the latter inducing property iv: domain knowledge). The description lists each database's logical name and schema; the hints file flags the transformations applied and any domainspecific definitions. Both are shown in the walkthrough in Section 3.3.

Queries and Answers. DAB contains 104 queries, each incorporating at least two of the four properties. A query comprises a natural-language question, a ground-truth answer (derived from the pretransformation data), and a validation script : a Python function that takes the agent's free-form response, normalizes it (e.g., trimming whitespace, lower-casing), and returns True or False by checking whether the ground truth appears within the normalized string. Validation scripts are bespoke per queryaccording to the answer type as follow:

- Numeric answers: we check whether the response contains a value within a predefined tolerance range of the ground truth.
- Single-valued answers (e.g., a book title): the ground truth appears as a substring of the response.
- Alternative valid formats: some answers are semantically equivalent to the ground truth but formatted differently. For example, ETF names may appear with or without their share-class suffix (e.g., 'Vanguard S&amp;P 500 ETF' vs. 'Vanguard S&amp;P 500 ETF VOO'). Since these differ only slightly, we compute the Levenshtein distance between the response and the ground truth and accept it if below a threshold (on average, 20% of the answer's length).
- Set-valued answers (e.g., a list of book titles): every element must appear, each checked by the single-answer rule above.
- Dictionary-valued answers (e.g., book titles with their average ratings): every key must appear, and each value must appear within a surrounding window of its key, with keys and values checked by the single-answer rule above.

Our validation scripts check whether the response contains the complete correct answer, even if it also contains incorrect information. Detecting additional incorrect information would require manual review or an LLM judge, making evaluation not scalable or deterministic. Two authors jointly write each query, its ground truth, and its validation script. To verify DAB, we continue the following process until all reviewers reach consensus:

- (i) Two authors independently review every dataset, solve every query, and test every validation script, using helpful tools (e.g., Claude for domain knowledge).
- (ii) They compare their findings and reconcile disagreements. We classify disagreements into the following two types and resolve by root cause:
- Dataset or query disagreements arise almost entirely from ambiguous wording. We clarify the query and ask another author to solve each revision until the intended answer is unambiguous.
- Validation script disagreements arise when the script misses valid answer formats or edge cases. We identify the missing cases and refine the script to handle them (e.g., Levenshtein distance to tolerate minor string variations).

## 4 Experiments

We evaluate three frontier LLM agents on DAB (5 trials per query each); the best agent (GPT5.5) reaches only 57% pass@1, no agent exceeds 70% pass@5, and one dataset ( patents ) is never solved. The rest of this section covers the setup (Section 4.1), main results (Section 4.2), ablations on dataset descriptions and hints (Section 4.3), and failure modes (Section 4.4). All agent trajectories are released 2 .

## 4.1 Setup

LLM Agents. We test three frontier LLMs, each paired with a state-of-the-art harness -an orchestration layer that wraps an LLM in a loop with some tools and default prompts, shown to substantially improve agent accuracy over fixed LLM API calls [1]. We enable all built-in tools for each harness. Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (Anthropic) uses the Claude Code harness [2, 3], and GPT5.5 (OpenAI Azure Foundry) uses the Codex harness [34]. Gemini-3.1-Pro (Google)'s default harness, Gemini CLI, has no extensible SDK [14], so we implement the state-of-the-art ReAct harness [45] with four tools-list\_db , query\_db , execute\_python , and return\_answer ; full tool signatures and prompt templates are in Section B. Individual tool calls time out after 600s; tool results larger than 10,000 characters are written to disk so agents can read them back. All parameters are set to provider defaults. We disable network access to prevent agents from loading external data (e.g., agnews ground-truth labels from Hugging Face) to obtain correct answers. For brevity, we hereafter name each agent by its model alone, omitting its harness.

Metrics. We measure accuracy via pass@ k [7], with n = 5 trials per query per agent and c correct: pass@ k = 1 -( n -c k ) / ( n k ) . All averages are stratified -per query, then per dataset, then across the 17 datasets-so larger datasets don't dominate. We also report cost (USD) and trajectory statistics (iterations, tool calls). The evaluation totals 4,680 trials at $4,346.

| Claude-Sonnet-4.6                         |         30.5 |          30.3 |          10.3 |            11.2 |
| GPT-5.5                                   |         16.3 |          12.7 |           9.2 |             2.3 |
| Gemini-3.1-Pro                            |         23.4 |          24.9 |          10.1 |            13.8 |
| Hardest query (highest per-query average) |              |               |               |                 |
| Claude-Sonnet-4.6                         |        160.0 |         159.0 |          38.5 |           102.5 |

Table 3 reports per-dataset breakdowns; no agent solves any query in patents . Figure 4 plots pass@ k as a function of k : agent rankings are stable, but the best agent still reaches only 70% pass@5 .

Cost-efficiency. Figure 3 plots total API cost against pass@1 (per-dataset breakdown in Table 3). Gemini-3.1-Pro offers the best cost-accuracy tradeoff at $294 total (52% pass@1). GPT-5.5 costs 1 . 6 × more for +5 pp accuracy, and Claude-Sonnet4.6 costs 2 . 4 × more yet is the least accurate. cve is the costliest dataset for every agent: it contains 95 MB of unstructured vulnerability records that agents pull into context to clean and join, and only GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.1-Pro answer a few of its queries correctly.

Trajectory patterns. Table 4 reports iterations and tool calls per trajectory, broken down into database queries ( list\_db / query\_db for ReAct; DBCLIssuch as duckdb , sqlite3 , psql , mongosh , or Python scripts importing only DB-related packages ( duckdb , sqlite3 , psycopg2 , pymongo ) for Claude Code and Codex) and Python executions ( execute\_python for ReAct; all other Python scripts for Claude Code and Codex). We highlight two takeaways.

Takeaway: Writing larger programs upfront is more costefficient than step-by-step exploration.

GPT-5.5 typically solves each query with one large Python program that inspects schemas, queries the database, and aggregates results in a single process. Claude-Sonnet-4.6 splits the same work into many smaller commands: a 0.9:1 DB-to-Python ratio versus 4:1 for GPT-5.5. For instance, on cve /query1, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 needs five Python executions to explore the database while GPT-5.5 does so in one. This pattern largely explains the cost gap: Claude-Sonnet-4.6 costs $705 at 48% pass@1, while GPT-5.5 costs $484 at 57%. Note that Gemini-3.1-Pro's DB-to-Python ratio is not directly comparable, since its ReAct harness exposes Python as a dedicated tool whereas Claude Code and Codex invoke Python via bash.

Takeaway: Parallel tool calling is underutilized, but could improve latency and cost.

Multi-database workloads in DAB would benefit from issuing tool calls in parallel, since each source can be queried independently. Exploratory calls (schema lookups, sample queries) are an especially natural fit for parallelization, and they make up a large fraction of trajectories: 51% for GPT-5.5, 39% for Claude-Sonnet-4.6, and 22% for Gemini3.1-Pro (Table 11). A single iteration may issue multiple tool calls in parallel, which is why some agents in Table 4 have fewer iterations than tool calls. However, all three agents parallelize on fewer than 10% of turns: Claude-Sonnet-4.6 most often (8.2%), followed by GPT-5.5 (5.2%) and Gemini3.1-Pro (5.1%). When they do parallelize, GPT5.5 and Gemini-3.1-Pro occasionally issue large bursts-up to 16 and 100 concurrent calls in a single turn.

We also ran a shared-harness experiment to evaluate different models, pairing ReAct with GPT 5.2, Claude Opus 4.6, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Due to budget limits, we used the 54 least expensive queries across 12 datasets, with five trials per model per query. Pass@1/pass@5 is 29%/44% for GPT 5.2, 55%/69% for Claude Opus 4.6, and 60%/75% for Gemini 3.1 Pro (details in Appendix C).

## 4.3 Ablations

The main experiments give each agent both dataset descriptions (databases, tables, schemas) and 'hints' that describe our induced data quality issues. Here, we perform two ablations: removing hints only ('w/o hints') and removing both descriptions and hints ('w/o desc+hints'), with 5 trials per query in each.

Table 5: Average pass@1, total cost (USD), and per-trial tool calls under each ablation, with the difference vs. the full-info setting in parentheses. Green : highest pass@1 across agents per row.

| Setting                     | Acc          | Cost        | #Tools      |
|-----------------------------|--------------|-------------|-------------|
| Claude-Sonnet-4.6 w/o hints | 0.50 (+0.02) | $670 (-$35) | 29.0 (-1.3) |
| w/o desc+hints              | 0.43 (-0.05) | $686 (-$19) | 37.9 (+7.6) |
| GPT-5.5 w/o hints           | 0.58 (+0.01) | $483 (-$1)  | 11.3 (-1.4) |
| w/o desc+hints              | 0.55 (-0.02) | $453 (-$31) | 15.8 (+3.1) |
| Gemini-3.1-Pro w/o hints    | 0.48 (-0.04) | $280 (-$14) | 25.6 (+0.7) |
| w/o desc+hints              | 0.47 (-0.05) | $299 (+$5)  | 34.2 (+9.3) |

Accuracy and cost. Table 5 reports the average pass@1, total cost, and per-trial tool calls under each ablation; the per-dataset breakdown is in Section D. Removing hints or descriptions sometimes decreases accuracy (as expected, since the agent has less information) and sometimes increases it: hints apply to the entire dataset, so when a particular query doesn't need a particular hint, the agent can be 'misled'. For example, on crmarenapro /query12, the agent sees a hint about join-key corruption-which actually applies to other queries in this dataset, not query12-and assumes its initial (correct) answer is wrong because it didn't clean for that corruption, so it reports a different, incorrect answer. Under 'w/o hints', the agent has no such suspicion and answers correctly in 2/5 trials. Across the board, however, accuracy shifts are marginal: pass@1 moves by at most 5 pp in either direction. Costs also shift only modestly, between -6% and +2% across agents and conditions.

Tool use. Unsurprisingly, removing the description ('w/o desc+hints') drives all three agents to issue more tool calls on average+3 to +9 per trial-as they probe schemas and surface data quality issues themselves. Removing hints alone has little effect ( ± 1 call). Interestingly, sometimes removing hints actually decreases exploration. For example, on usaspending , where a join column is corrupted in ways that require row-by-row reasoning, in the main experiment, agents consider the hint and issue many tool calls to do that reasoning (ClaudeSonnet-4.6: 53.5/trial, Gemini-3.1-Pro: 48.9/trial). But under 'w/o hints', they never discover the corruptions, issue far fewer tool calls (39.4 and 22.7 respectively), and return the wrong answer.

## 4.4 Error Analysis

Wealso analyze failed trajectories to identify where the agents are breaking down.

Methodology. Two authors examined 30 failed trajectories from the bookreview dataset and defined five failure modes specific to data agents. To classify presence of failure modes at scale, we used GPT-5 as an LLM judgeover one incorrect trajectory per query per agent in the main experiment, yielding 196 annotated trajectories. The LLM judge doesn't perform open ended error analysis; it determines whether a trajectory exhibits each human defined failure mode, following prior work in agent evaluation [6, 32, 53]. We follow the procedure used by Terminal Bench. The full annotation prompt and per-agent breakdown are in Section E.2, and trajectories illustrating each FM appear in Section E.3. The failure modes are:

- FM1 Fails before planning : the agent makes no attempt-either returning None as its tool call ( FM1(no\_tool\_call) ) or refusing without invoking any tool ( FM1(other) ).
- FM2 Incorrect plan : the agent's plan cannot produce the correct answer even if executed perfectlye.g., averaging book-level averages within a decade rather than averaging the underlying review ratings directly.
- FM3 Incorrect data selection : the plan is right but the agent queries the wrong source-e.g., checking the description column for a book's language when the details column holds it.
- FM4 Incorrect implementation : plan and data are right but execution is wrong-e.g., a regex intended to extract a publication year inadvertently matches an ISBN segment from details .
- FM5 Runtime error : API failures (non-200 HTTP responses, tool-call array overflows, 'service unavailable') or request timeouts ( &gt; 600s).

Results. Figure 5 and Figure 6 in Section E.1 show the failure-mode breakdown across all 1,560 trajectories in the main experiment. We report two takeaways below.

Takeaway: Agents typically select the right data, but fail at planning the computation or implementing it correctly.

Among the trajectories that completed but returned incorrect answers (Figure 6), FM4 (incorrect implementation) is the most common at 57%, followed by FM2 (incorrect plan) at 31%, FM3 (incorrect data selection) at 11%, and FM1 (other) at 1%. The low rate of FM3 indicates that agents generally identify the correct tables and columns; the dominant challenge is deciding what to compute and computing it correctly. Together, FM2 and FM4 account for 90% of incorrect answers.

Takeaway: All agents rely on regex for text extraction and fail when it isn't expressive enough.

Whenagents need to parse text fields-e.g., pulling a date out of a sentence-they default to authoring and executing a regex; only Claude-Sonnet-4.6 ever calls an LLM-based extractor (and only on agnews ). This breaks down on DAB's text-heavy datasets. For example, on patents (0% pass@1 for every agent), dates appear in many naturallanguage forms (e.g., 'dated 5th March 2019', 'March the 18th, 2019'), and no regex the agents write covers all of them. In another example, on pancancer\_atlas , a regex for MALE matches inside FEMALE and mislabels gender. Perhaps exposing dedicated extraction tools (e.g., date parsers, NER, LLM-based extractors) as first-class tools, rather than forcing agents to author them ad hoc, could unlock many of DAB's hardest queries.

While our quantitative analysis is intended to compare the relative prevalence of the failure modes-rather than estimate the exact fraction of trajectories exhibiting each failure mode-to further adjudicate GPT-5's judge and validate the takeaways above, we ran two more experiments:

- Human validation: One author reviewed 30 trajectories, 10 per agent. 20 labels (67%) match the GPT-5 judge exactly; 3 (10%) partially match because the human assigns extra failure modes; and 7 (23%) disagree. Importantly, the human labels rank failure-mode prevalence the same as the judge.
- Agreement across LLM judges: We re-annotated all trajectories with GPT-5.4 to measure judge agreement. Cohen's κ is 0.80 for FM1 and 0.420.46 for FM2-FM4, indicating strong or moderate agreement. More importantly, both judges give the same ordering: FM2 (42% with GPT-5.4, 31% with GPT-5) and FM4 (44%, 57%) dominate, FM3 follows (13%, 11%), and FM1 is rare (1% for both).

## 5 Conclusion

We presented DAB, the first benchmark for evaluating data agents on realistic, multi-database queries. Grounded in a formative study of enterprise workloads, DAB comprises 104 queries across 17 datasets and 4 database systems. Even the best frontier agent achieves only 57% pass@1, and 90% of failures stem from incorrect plans or incorrect implementations rather than data selection. DAB represents a significant step forward for data agent evaluation, and we hope it helps the community build data agents that can be trusted in production.

## 6 Limitations

DAB reflects several tradeoffs we made during construction. First, DAB uses four open-source database systems (PostgreSQL, MongoDB, SQLite, and DuckDB) so that it can be run without commercial licenses; enterprise deployments commonly involve proprietary systems such as Oracle, Snowflake, and Databricks, which introduce additional challenges (e.g., vendor-specific SQL dialects, access-control policies) that DAB does not yet capture. Second, all queries are analytical and read-only-the benchmark does not cover transactional workloads in which agents must insert, update, or delete records. In fact, data systems typically use separate benchmarks for distinct workload classes rather than a single benchmark intended to cover them all. For example, analytical and transactional workloads are conventionally evaluated using TPC-H and TPC-C, respectively. Hex, a popular data agent startup, has multiple internal benchmarks for different workloads, such as warehouse analytics [16] and chart generation [15].

Third, every query has a single deterministic answer, which enables fully automatic evaluation but excludes open-ended analytical questions (Section 3.1) and queries requiring statistical modeling or machine-learning workflows; existing data science benchmarks [18, 23, 24] already target these capabilities. Fourth, DAB excludes queries that depend on external APIs (email clients, web search, third-party data providers); our formative study found these common in production, but live endpoints break reproducibility. Moreover, live external data introduce data quality issues that we cannot continuously identify and correct, making it difficult to evaluate agents fairly or ensure that the data meets the expectations established in our formative studies. Fifth, DAB contains 104 queries across 17 datasets-comparable in size to other carefully curated benchmarks (e.g., FrontierMath [13], TerminalBench [32])-but does not yet cover every domain or database system encountered in production. Despite manual verification and independent review by different authors (Section 3.2), some queries may be ambiguous or hints may contain inconsistencies. We plan to expand DAB over time and welcome community contributions and corrections. We hope the community develops benchmarks for additional data agent workloads, and we plan to extend DAB to cover more workloads over time.

## 7 Ethical Considerations

Our formative-study interviews and data-handling protocol were approved by our institution's IRB; participants gave informed consent, and we release no proprietary customer data, schemas, or queries. DAB is built from open-source datasets used consistent with their licenses (Section 3.2) and contains no PII. We release DAB's transformation scripts, validation scripts, and evaluation code under the MIT license; the transformed datasets are released for research use only, consistent with the licenses of their underlying sources.

We used LLMs at several points in this workGPT-4o to embed structured attributes into freeform text during dataset construction (with all transformations author-verified to preserve deterministic ground truth), GPT-5 to annotate which failure modes appear in each incorrect trajectory (Figure 6), and Claude Haiku to classify tool calls as exploratory or analytical (Table 11).

The total experiment cost is $4,346 (Section 4.2). This is a substantial figure, especially for university research labs, and it is a real barrier to reproducibility: re-running the full evaluation, or evaluating a new agent on DAB, takes thousands of dollars. To partially mitigate this, we release all agent trajectories and code so that downstream analyses can be performed without re-running the experiments.

We caution that accuracy on DAB does not imply deployment readiness, particularly in regulated domains.

## A Benchmark Construction Details

## A.1 Interview Protocol and Sample Response

We solicited each enterprise's data-agent workload through a structured questionnaire. For each enterprise, we asked the analysts and engineers building the data agent to provide:

1. the natural-language queries their end users pose (or wish to pose) to a data agent;
2. the schemas of their data sources, including the database system each source uses (e.g., PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Salesforce, vector store);
3. where each piece of data is stored, including overlapping or redundant data across systems;
4. the join keys between tables, both within a single database and across databases; and
5. for each example query, a plan describing how an analyst would manually perform the joins, transformations, and any text extractions needed to answer it.

Below we reproduce an anonymized sample response from one enterprise, an enterprise projectmanagement SaaS platform (comparable in scope to products such as Asana or Monday).

## Data sources.

1. Platform database (PostgreSQL): customers , users , projects , tasks , feature\_usage .
2. Support database (PostgreSQL): agents , tickets , ticket\_responses .
3. Salesforce : accounts , opportunities , contacts .
4. Billing database (MongoDB): invoices , usage\_metrics .
5. Documentation (vector database): documents with text and embeddings.

The response also provided example rows and join keys for each source (e.g., customers.customer\_id ↔ users.customer\_id ;

Salesforce accounts.Name fuzzily matches customers.company\_name ).

Example queries. The response provided dozens of queries organized into five categories. We list a representative example from each, with the analyst's stated plan.

- (1) Joining across data sources. Exact (1:1) join. 'Which enterprise-plan customers have raised a support ticket in the last 30 days?' Plan: filter customers by plan\_type=enterprise , join with users on customer\_id , query tickets by these user\_id s with created\_date in the last 30 days.

Programmatic transform join. 'Which Salesforce accounts correspond to our platform customers?' Plan: normalize company names in both customers and Salesforce accounts (strip 'Inc', 'Corp' suffixes; lowercase); join on normalized names.

Fuzzy/semantic join. 'Which customers mentioned in Salesforce opportunities are the same as our existing platform customers?' Plan: fuzzy string matching to reconcile variations such as 'International Business Machines' vs. 'IBM'.

- (2) Bulk semantic operations. Classification. 'Does our average ticket resolution time differ for production vs. non-production issues?' Plan: classify each ticket from tickets.description using an LLM; aggregate resolution\_time per class.

Extraction. 'Which software versions have reported the most issues?' Plan: extract version numbers from ticket descriptions (e.g., 'v2.1.3') with regex/NER; group by version.

Clustering. 'What are the top issues that keep recurring?' Plan: semantically cluster ticket descriptions and rank clusters by frequency.

Generation/summarization. 'Generate a monthly support performance report with key insights.'

- (3) Search. 'If someone is running into XYZ error, what should we do?' Plan: vector-search the documentation database and the resolved-ticket archive; combine results.
- (4) Domain knowledge. 'Which deals are 'at risk'?' Plan: apply this company's definition of 'at risk'-opportunities with Probability &lt; 50% closing within 30 days, or accounts with billing issues or declining usage metrics.
- (5) Open-ended. 'What should I do to improve my support process?' (Excluded from DAB because no single correct answer.)

## ## Transfer Count Policy

- Definition: The number of instances a case was reassigned or transferred from one agent to another. Each transfer from agent A to agent B adds to the transfer count for agent A.

- In the queries that specify 'agents managed/queries x cases'-this filter applies to both the first agent that the case was first assigned to and the agent that the case was transferred to. This means that if an agent has 2 cases that was initially assigned to itself by admin and 1 case transferred from another agent, a filter like 'handled/managed at least 3 cases' would not filter this agent out.

- For cases that have NOT been transferred to an other agent, there will be only ONE 'Owner Assignment', and for those that have been transferred, there will be MORE THAN ONE 'Owner Assignment'.

(10) In the past four months, which agent had the lowest average handle time for those processing more than one case? Return only the Id of the agent.

## ## Handle Time Policy

- Definition: The duration taken to close a case. Specifically, it is the time from when a case is opened to when it is closed.

- In the queries that specify 'agents managed/queries x cases'-this filter applies to both the first agent that the case was first assigned to and the agent that the case was transferred to. This means that if an agent has 2 cases that was initially assigned to itself by admin and 1 case transferred from another agent, a filter like 'handled/managed at least 3 cases' would not filter this agent out.

- When computing handle time, we do not compute handle time for cases that have been transferred to other agents.

- For cases that have NOT been transferred to an other agent, there will be only ONE 'Owner Assignment', and for those that have been transferred, there will be MORE THAN ONE 'Owner Assignment'.

## A.4 Workload Properties

To show the mapping between the datasets and the workload properties we observed in formative study, we report in Table 7 which queries in each dataset exhibit P2, ill formatted join keys; P3, unstructured text transformation; and P4, domain knowledge. Each cell lists the relevant query IDs, followed by the number of queries in parentheses. We omit P1, integration across heterogeneous databases, from the table because all 104 queries exhibit it.

Section 3.2 already describes and illustrates the four techniques used to introduce P2 and P3. Here, we name these techniques explicitly and show where each is applied:

- T1: Rename a shared identifier across tables, such that the same entity is identified by columns with different names.
- T2: Apply row specific corruptions to join keys, including prefixes, OCR like substitutions, whitespace, and special characters.
- T3: Embed values needed to answer a query within unstructured text and remove the original structured column.
- T4: Express numeric values in varied free text formats.

Some datasets exhibit P2 or P3 'natively,' or without a synthetic transformation. Specifically, agnews natively requires article classification, mu-sic\_brainz\_20k natively requires entity resolution, and stockindex natively requires mapping full stock exchange names to their abbreviations. Table 8 maps each dataset to the techniques used to introduce P2 and P3, or marks the property as native.

## E.2 FMAnnotation Prompt

Below is the prompt template for GPT-5 to annotate FM1 (other) , FM2 , FM3 , and FM4 for a failed trajectory.

- 1 You are given a trace of a FAILED task executed by a data agent, along with the task query and the ground -truth answer. Your task is to diagnose WHY the agent's final answer does not match the ground truth using the failure modes FM1 -4 defined below. 2 3 The agent had access to the following tools: 4 -list\_db: list tables in a database 5 -query\_db: execute SQL queries 6 -execute\_python: run Python code for data processing 7 -return\_answer: terminate and return the final answer 8 9 The trace records the complete interaction between the data agent and the available tools. That is, the trace contains: 10 -Exploratory tool calls (trial-anderror) 11 -Tool calls that directly contributed to the final answer 12 13 ## IMPORTANT INSTRUCTIONS: 14 1. First, identify ONLY the tool calls whose outputs were used (directly or indirectly) to produce the final answer. Ignore abandoned, failed, or exploratory tool calls that did not affect the final output. 15 2. Base your failure analysis ONLY on those contributing tool calls. 16 3. You must mark at least one failure mode as "yes". By default, select exactly one failure mode-the most specific one that best explains why the final answer is incorrect. Select multiple failure modes only if the failure cannot be adequately explained by any single mode alone (i.e., each selected mode captures a distinct, necessary cause visible in the contributing tool calls). 17 4. Only mark a failure mode as "yes" if you can point to a concrete example in the trace. 18 5. Provide a single-sentence summary explaining the failure, explicitly referencing the trace behavior. 19 20 ## FAILURE MODELS 21 FM1 -Fails Before Planning 22 Definition: 23 -The agent does not attempt to solve the query. 24 Example: 25 -The agent does not issue any tool
- calls. 26 27 FM2 - Incorrect Plan 28 Definition: 29 -The agent attempts to solve the user 's query, but the PLAN (i.e., the logical structure) of the solution is wrong. That is, even if all steps were executed perfectly (e.g ., correct data selection, correct implementation, no execution errors), the plan cannot produce the ground-truth answer. 30 Examples: 31 -Missing operations specified or implied by the user. 32 -Adding constraints not requested by the user. 33 -Stops early and returns an answer before all requirements of the query are completed. 34 35 FM3 - Correct Plan, Wrong Data Selection 36 Definition: 37 -The agent follows a theoretically correct plan for answering the user's query, but selects incorrect data sources in its implementation, such that the required information exists but is retrieved from the wrong database , table, collection, column, or field. 38 Example: 39 -Using an incorrect column in a selection or filtering condition ( e.g., a WHERE clause references a column that does not represent the queried attribute, even though the correct column exists elsewhere in the schema). 40 -Querying or joining a table that does not represent the queried entity, despite the correct table exists elsewhere in the schema. 41 42 FM4 - Correct Plan and Data Selection, Incorrect Implementation 43 Definition: 44 The agent the correct plan and selects the correct tables and columns, but implements the computation incorrectly. 45 Examples: 46 -Arithmetic errors, such as computing an aggregate with an incorrect formula (e.g., dividing by the number of unique entities rather than the total number of contributing entities or records when calculating an overall average). 47 -Incorrect regular expressions or parsing rules, such that extracted values include unintended matches or miss required values (e.g., patterns that capture unrelated numbers or fail to match the intended tokens).

```
48 -Parsing errors, such as using unsupported syntax, improper escaping, or assumptions about the execution environment that cause incorrect behavior or failed execution. 49 -Incorrect join implementation, where the agent applies an invalid join condition or fails to normalize or transform identifiers before joining, even though the trace indicates awareness that normalization or alignment is required. 50 51 ## QUERY 52 {{uesr_query}} 53 54 ## GROUND-TRUTH ANSWER 55 {{ground_truth_answer}} 56 57 ## FAILED TRACE 58 {{failed_trajectory}} 59 60 ## OUTPUT FORMAT 61 Your output MUST follow this exact format, starting after @@ and ending before @@: 62 63 @@ 64 A. Freeform text summary of the failure: 65 <one sentence> 66 B. Failure modes encountered: 67 FM1: <yes or no> 68 FM2: <yes or no> 69 FM3: <yes or no> 70 FM4: <yes or no> 71 @@
```

## E.3 Examples of Failed Trajectories

Examples in this section are drawn from the bookreview dataset, with the following description and hints:

```
1 DATABASE DESCRIPTION: 2 You are working with two databases to solve this query. 3 4 Here are the descriptions of these two databases: 5 6 1. books_database 7 -This database is stored in a PostgreSQL database and contains Amazon book information including descriptions, price, details, title, etc. up to 2023. 8 -This database consists of one table: 9 -books_info: 10 -Fields: 11 -title (str): Book title 12 -subtitle (str): Book subtitle 13 -author (str): Book author(s) 14 -rating_number (int): Total
```

## E.3.1 FM2 : Incorrect Plan for Averaging

## Query. Q1

Analysis. This trajectory fails due to an incorrect averaging plan: it computes decade-level averages by averaging per-book average ratings, whereas the query requires directly averaging all ratings within each decade. Specifically, the final answer in Line

The agent first computes per-book average ratings-treating each purchase\_id as a book identifier-when processing review records (Line 38). ## E.3.2 FM2 : Missing Operations

## Query. Q2

Analysis. This trajectory fails by missing a required constraint: the selected books must have an average rating of exactly 5.0. Specifically, the final answer in Line 591 is produced by the execute\_python tool call in Line 561, which depends on a prior execute\_python call in Line 525, itself derived from a query\_db call in Line 113. All three calls contributing to the final answer ignore the constraint that the average rating must equal 5.0.

## E.3.3 FM2 : Adding Operations

Query. Q3

Analysis. This trajectory fails by introducing unwarranted operations: it adds LIMIT 200 when retrieving review records (Line 38) and LIMIT 500 when retrieving book records (Line 50), while the query does not require any such limits.

## E.3.4 FM3 : Incorrect Column Selection

## Query. Q2

Analysis. This trajectory fails by selecting an incorrect column. To filter books written in English, the agent relies on columns other than the correct one (i.e., details ) in the books\_info table, although the database description already indicates details as the correct column (Line 39). Specifically, in Line 125 of the trajectory below, the agent attempts to search for 'English' using details , description , and other columns. However, the book records it inspects originate from var\_call\_he4GeOzFNhdoBfpZPxkmX09E (Line 110), which is produced by the query\_db call in Line 51 executing SELECT book\_id, title, author, categories, description FROM books\_info; This query does not retrieve the details column. In effect, the agent searches for 'English' using columns other than the correct one ( details ), leading to failure.

## E.3.5 FM4 : Incorrect Regular Expression

## Query. Q1

Analysis. This trajectory fails due to an overly permissive regular expression. The agent uses a pattern to extract any four-digit string starting with 19 or 20 (Line 66) and then selects the smallest extracted value (Line 73) as the publication year. This approach may incorrectly extract 1932 from an ISBN rather than the true publication year, 2004 , as in the example shown in Line 17.
